Canadian Camping 










RETROSPECT 

and 

REFLECTIONS 

Another camping season has passed. 
We hope it was as pleasant and success¬ 
ful for all members of the Canadian 
Camping Association as it was for us. 
We trust that most of those fine plans 
and aspirations, for which we held such 
high hopes last spring, were realized. It 
is perhaps too much to expect that all 
our goals should be met, but we have 
reason to be satisfied if steady progress 
is being made towards their final 
realization. 

Now, pleasant thoughts of what the 
past season meant to our campers and 
ourselves must give way to planning for 
the next summer. This is the season to 
take a critical look at all phases of our 
camp operation. It is time now to de¬ 
cide what changes and additions should 
be made in staff programme, buildings 
and equipment for the 1959 season. 

In our case, we decide first what ad¬ 
ditions and improvements are to be 
made to the physical plant. No diffi¬ 
culty is found in mapping out sufficient 
work to keep our two-man maintenance 
staff fully occupied until snow flies, and 
again from mid-March to camp open¬ 
ing. During the winter and spring, the 
senior staff will meet regularly to con¬ 
sider selection and training of counsel¬ 
lors and junior counsellors, camp pro¬ 
gramme and all other matters related 
to the efficient operation of camp. 


Toronto , Canada , December 1958 


EDITORIAL 


F. M. Van Wagner 
President } Canadian Camping Association 


Perhaps this is also a good time to 
again consider our camp objectives. 
What is it we hope to achieve? What 
do we want campers to gain from their 
camping experience? Have we a good 
answer to the parent who asks “Why 
should my children go to camp? We 
have a country home on a nice lake 
where they have swimming, canoeing, 
sailing, tennis and many other things 
camp can give them”. We, of course, 
believe that these children are most 
fortunate, but still have no adequate 
substitute for the good summer camp. 
Frequently, the children, having heard 
from friends how much fun camp is, 
may make the important decision to go 
to camp. Usually camp will meet their 
highest expectations, and parents, when 
visiting camp, are fully convinced that 
their children are getting much that 
they could not have gained elsewhere. 

While many parents and children 
fully appreciate the value of organized 
summer camps, there are many who 
do not. There is still a great need for 
continuing a general educational pro¬ 
gramme, using all means at our disposal 
to create wide public appreciation of 
the real value of organized camping. 

At least one way we can all contri¬ 
bute to this end is to support the 
Canadian Camping Association through 
active participation in our Provincial 
Camping Associations. 

—• 


9 



Presented to the Quebec Camping Association on the occasion of their Annual Conference 

in Montreal, April, 1958. 


CAMPS 

AND CONSERVATION 


by Prof. Reynold Carlson, 

Professor of Recreation, 

School of Health, Physical Education and 
Recreation 

University of Indiana 


As we in the Americas become in¬ 
creasingly nations of city dwellers with 
more money, more leisure, and more 
freedom to travel, we as a people are 
turning more and more to the out-of- 
doors for rest, release from tensions, 
inspiration, and participation in those 
pursuits that call for self-reliance, in¬ 
genuity, and initiative. There is every 
reason to believe that this exodus is only 
in its beginning stages and will increase 
as years go by. There seems to be some¬ 
thing deep in human beings that calls 
them back to the woods, fields, lakes 
mountains, and streams. It is this desire 
that brings our children to camp, and 
calls millions of people out of doors for 
summer vacations, to fish, canoe, hike, 
climb mountains, lie lazily in the sun, 
swim, or engage in a hundred other 
pursuits. 

Increasingly our people are con¬ 
sumers of the land rather than pro¬ 
ducers. While the percentage of our 
people who grow the food, fibre, and 
wood become less and less, the percen¬ 
tage who use our resources for leisure 
pursuits becomes greater and greater. 

The great surge out of doors has 
brought its problems. Among them are 
the reckless use of natural resources, 
the lack of understanding of the world 


of nature, and vandalism sufficient to 
close much private land to visitors and 
to cause consternation among adminis¬ 
trators of public property. 

How can we conserve our unspoiled 
resources so that they may continue to 
be sources of inspiration and recreation 
to future generations? What respon¬ 
sibility do we as camp leaders have to 
help children attain satisfaction out of 
doors but also to assure such satisfac¬ 
tion to their successors? 

Through the years ahead, camping 
for children will doubtless assume grow¬ 
ing importance, both as an outdoor 
experience in group living and as an 
educational experience through which 
attitudes, skills and interests may be 
learned that will have important con¬ 
sequences to the individual and to 
society. 

Those of us engaged in organized 
camping professionally believe that the 
camp is one of the most effective situa¬ 
tions in which we can place children 
to influence behavior. We recognize 
that, in the child’s mind, camp must be 
fun and adventure and that, if the aura 
of fun and adventure is lost, camping 
will no longer be the valuable educa¬ 
tional experience we cherish for child¬ 
ren. 


10 


Canadian Camping 


We, as camp leaders, consider camp 
the place in which to teach a great 
variety of things. We talk of developing 
personal qualities, group relationships, 
nature knowledge,- health habits, inter¬ 
national understanding, self-expression, 
arts and crafts,. music, and physical 
skills. Sometimes it seems that camps 
‘try to do everything under the sun and 
expect in a few short weeks to change 
patterns of behaviour that have been 
years in developing. 

Certainly these things have important 
places in the camp programme. How¬ 
ever, some things can be accomplished 
better in the camp setting than else¬ 
where ; while still other things are 
unique to camping and can be achieved 
only in camp. If we can always 
remember that camp is simple group 
living out of doors and that some of the 
attitudes and learnings we desire to de¬ 
velop in campers are by-products of this 
simple living, we may make our greatest 
contribution to the education of 
campers. 

It is my opinion that there is no 
better place than the organized camp in 
which to develop the attitudes, habits, 
and skills that will bring about the 
wisest use of our natural resources. 

A camp’s responsibilities in conserva¬ 
tion education lie in four fields. First, 
the camp can contribute towards the 
establishment of valuable daily habits— 
habits which, though small in them¬ 
selves, contribute towards the beauty 
and usefulness of the land. Do campers 
learn to keep their living areas clean? 
Do they pick up their litter? Do they 
make proper disposal of garbage and 
other waste? Do they use native mat¬ 
erials with care, even when taking sticks 
for outdoor broiling? Do they care for 
their fires cautiously, even when there 
may seem to be no danger of forest fire? 
Camp leaders may be careless and edu¬ 
cate wrongly, or they may, by example 


and instruction, instil a concern for 
the out-of-doors, and encourage habits 
that will have far-reaching effects. 

Second, camps have a responsibility 
to help children achieve some know¬ 
ledge of the processes upon which life 
depends. I do not mean that a course 
in biology should be given in camp. 
Rather, the camper should develop the 
ability to observe the world about him 
and should begin to understand its 
manifold inter-relationships. Stars, 
weather, rocks, plants, and animals 
make up his natural environment. 
They are at hand to be enjoyed, ob¬ 
served, and properly used. 

Third, all of our camp craft activities 
should be conducted with a considera¬ 
tion for the wise use of resources. Crafts 
using native materials provide oppor¬ 
tunities to develop respect for materials 
and their sources. 

Fourth, camps can help children de¬ 
velop appreciations. Appreciations are 
intangible and personal, and we do not 
know much about how they are de¬ 
veloped. However, we can place child¬ 
ren in situations where beauty can be 
enjoyed and can hope that appreciation 
may be caught through the attitudes 
of counsellors and other camp staff 
members. Through arts and crafts, 
through song, and through the spoken 
word, we have further opportunities to 
enlarge appreciations. Fortunate is the 
child who goes home from camp with 
a love of the world of nature, a per¬ 
ceptive curiosity about it, and a sense 
of its worth. 

Conservation is just a normal part of 
outdoor living. It is part and parcel 
of camping. Good camping has its first 
concern for what happens to the 
camper in the development of those at¬ 
titudes, skills, and interests that will be 
of value not only to him as an in¬ 
dividual but to the society in which he 
lives. 

—• 


Toronto , Canada , December 1958 


11 



AMONG 

OURSELVES 

By Russel F Brown 
Archdeacon of Quebec 

We were an odd outfit. There were 
about twenty-five of us, all shapes and 
sizes and varying in age from eighteen 
to forty. When we went up to Uni¬ 
versity some of us had visions of don¬ 
ning football togs or even, perhaps of 
going on parade with the G.O.T.C.; 
but here we were all dressed as Boy 
Scouts — bare knees and all — and 
gathering every week for stalking games 
in the ample woods near the College, 
pitching tents, building camp-fires, 
learning the art of bannock-making, 
(and trying to eat it!) and sampling for 
the first time steak cooked in ashes—we 
were a Rover Crew in action. I think 
some of us were a little taken aback by 
this wholly unexpected college activity; 
but if we had any private misgivings 
they were soon dissipated by our Leader 
whose patience and skill in the art of 
scout-craft quickly infected us with his 
enthusiasm for camping, and we began 
to see, what he saw so clearly, that it 
was a wonderful opportunity for em¬ 
bryo parsons to learn to give leadership 
to boys in all forms of out-door life, so 
that lads—and parsons too—could see 
that there was nothing anaemic about 
the Gospel of the Master. 

All this happened almost thirty years 
ago, in 1929, under the leadership of 
our new Dean of Divinity, Phillip Car¬ 
rington, who had come to Lennoxville 
from New Zealand in 1927. It was a 
sight, never to be forgotten, to watch 
our Leader demonstrate Maori dances 
and crys, and soon we were learning 
the rhythms, grimaces and sounds that 



The Most Reverend Philip Carrington , 
M.A., Litt.D.j D.C.L., S.T.D., D.D. 

Metropolitan of the Ecclesiastical Province of Canada 


went with them. Once, suitably un¬ 
dressed, a performance was given that 
rather stunned a polite audience who 
were wholly unprepared for this 
glimpse of divinity students in such un¬ 
usual action. 

This development at Bishop’s Uni¬ 
versity was the result of the long and 
varied background of Philip Carring¬ 
ton in New Zealand, Australia and 
in England: scouting was in his blood 
from the earliest days of B-P’s move¬ 
ment. Most of his spare time went into 
the encouragement of out-door life for 
boys. As a student at Canterbury Col¬ 
lege, University of New Zealand, he 
was Scoutmaster with St. Michael’s 
Church Troop at Christchurch and 
later, in England, with St. Paul’s Troop 
at Cambridge. Many a boy of those 
days owed his devotion to scouting to 
the inspired leadership of Philip Car¬ 
rington. It was during his college days 
in England that his camping experi¬ 
ments were published under the title 
“Boy Scouts’ Camp Book” with a pre¬ 
face by the Chief Scout. It proved to 


12 


Canadian Camping 


be a most popular and useful manual; 
a sixth edition was published in 1947 
and a further printing is contemplated. 
On his return to New Zealand he be¬ 
came Provincial Commissioner for Can¬ 
terbury, and Commissioner for Training 
Scout Officers in New Zealand. It was 
during this period, with his own parish 
troop at Kairaki on the Waimakiriri 
River that some of his most interesting 
and fruitful camping experiences took 
place. From New Zealand he went to 
Australia and it was there, while War¬ 
den of St. Barnabas College, Adelaide, 
that he first experimented with a Rover 
Crew made up of college students. All 
this varied experience laid the back¬ 
ground for the Bishop’s University ven¬ 
ture, and assured its success. 

Much might be written about Philip 
Carrington’s scholarship which has 
grown over the years, and of his many 
books which place him in the forefront 
of Anglican theologians, but nothing 
has abated his interest in scouting and 
young people. It was a surprise to no 
one that he was raised to the episcopacy. 
After eight short years the Dean of 
Divinity at Lennoxville became the 
seventh Bishop of Quebec, and in 1944 
he was elected Archbishop of Quebec 
and Metropolitan of the Ecclesiastical 
Province of Canada. 

During all these years the same pat¬ 
tern of emphasis on camping can be 
clearly seen, and to-day his Diocese is 
recognised as a leader in this field. The 
beginnings were small and unheralded. 
In the early days of his episcopacy, 
Bishop Carrington organized an Angli¬ 
can Boys’ Camp (known in the diocese 
as A.B.C.) at Leeds, Que. Here was an 
ideal setting that caught the imagina¬ 
tion of the boys. The old stone rectory, 
built by the Royal Engineers in the early 
years of the last century, became the 
centre of instruction; the grounds gave 
ample space for tents and sports, and 
the attractive little church nearby, as 


ancient as the old rectory, provided a 
focus for worship. The little Osgood 
River supplied the indispensable ‘swim¬ 
ming hole’. Many are the boys who can 
look back with gratitude to the weeks 
they spent at Leeds, and a number of 
them are to-day in the ministry of God’s 
Church because of their camping fel¬ 
lowship under the leadership of their 
Bishop. 

After some years the small beginning 
at Leeds was merged into a large under¬ 
taking. A handsome seven acre property 
on the edge of Lake Massiwippi at 
North Hatley came up for sale. On it 
were several fine buildings overlooking 
the lake: an ideal site for a camp. But 
the problem was money; there were no 
funds for its purchase. Twelve thousand 
dollars was being asked for it but when 
the owner learned that Bishop Carring¬ 
ton was interested it was offered for five 
thousand, and friends, impressed by his 
concern for camping, provided the 
money for its purchase. And so ‘Que¬ 
bec Lodge’ came into being. For a 
number of years it was a Girls’ and 
Young People’s Camp and ran concur¬ 
rently with A.B.C. at Leeds; then came 
the development that centered all these 
activities at North Hatley. This came 
about in an unusual and rather unex¬ 
pected way. As the Camp’s popularity 
grew and the numbers of campers in¬ 
creased year by year, it became appar¬ 
ent that Quebec Lodge had developed 
a ‘nuisance value.’ The nearby cot¬ 
tagers, all of whom were good friends of 
the Lodge, indicated that they would 
be happier if Quebec Lodge could find 
accommodation elsewhere and as an in¬ 
ducement one of them made an offer 
to buy the property for $30,000.00 cash. 
Such a figure called for serious con¬ 
sideration and after much investigation 
an alternative site was located on the 
other side of the lake—an extensive 
farm property of 145 acres; so the offer 

continued on page 31 


Toronto, Canada, December 1958

THE ART OF OUTDOOR LIVING 

A precis of the talk given by CHARLES 
STAFFORD of the Boy Scouts Association 3 
at the Quebec Camping Association Con¬ 
ference } April t 1958. 


What wonderful impressions that title 
conjures up—white water; the scent of 
pine and frying bacon mingling on the 
morning breeze; the feeling of really 
being alive tingling in every muscle and 
nerve of your body; the silence of lonely 
places, pregnant with noises you can 
not hear; and that peace which, coming 
from close contact with God’s gifts, 
passeth all understanding. 

However, it is not my intention to 
tell you how to live out of doors—that is 
something which can only be learned 
by doing, but rather to discover what 
is this art and what collectively we are 
doing about passing it on to our youth 
of today and tomorrow. 

The art of outdoor living, like any 
true art, orginates in the mind or an 
attitude of mind. Perhaps I can best 
explain this by comparing an explorer 
with a hypothetical tourist. The ex¬ 
plorer travels seeking whatever he can 
find and although he may never find 
that which he originally sought, he dis¬ 
covers so much else of interest and value 
that his own life is lived to the full and, 
to a greater or lesser degree, he justifies 
his existence. The tourist, on the other 
hand, goes places just for the sake of 
travelling, hoping to find relief from 
boredom but finding only criticism for 
everything that is different from 
“home”, and the only value reaped is 
the prestige he thinks he gains in his 
circle when he can boast of where he 
has been. 

The famous writer and exploring 
traveller, Robert Louis Stevenson, 
wrote, “To travel hopefully is a better 
thing than to arrive.” Isn’t this some¬ 


thing we are fast losing sight of? Are 
we not today far too concerned with 
possession, with arriving, rather than 
the journey? After all, when you “ar¬ 
rive” you have completed what you set 
out to do. Now what shall you do? 
Isn’t the planning, the preparation, and 
the anticipation, often as rewarding 
as the event itself? Sometimes the 
event may be even an anticlimax. 
I can remember a hike I went 
on many years ago as a Boy Scout; 
what the purpose was or where we 
planned to go I cannot now remember, 
but one part of the journey is vividly 
stamped on my mind. It was Spring¬ 
time, and we were climbing a long 
wooded slope in the Ghiltern Hills in 
pouring rain. Just as we approached 
the summit, we heard church bells peal 
out on the other side, and as we broke 
through the last of the trees, the rain 
stopped, the sun came out turning their 
driping young leaves into shining gold. 
There, unfolded before us rather like 
a scene for fairyland, was a long grassy 
slope leading down into a green valley 
with a stream shimmering along the 
bottom. Nestling under some trees 
stood a little village out of which poked 
the Norman tower of the church 
whose bells pealed so joyously. We 
were four teen-age boys but the miracle 
of the transformation stopped us dead 
in our tracks. 

You may say, “What has this to do 
with the art of outdoor living?” Simply 
this—he who would discover the art of 
outdoor living must first be an ex¬ 
plorer prepared to make the most of 
every opportunity each new experience 
presents and he must seek these enjoy- 


14 


Canadian Camping 



merits alone, or at most with only a 
few companions. More and more, man 
is becoming one of the masses, where 
individualism counts for less and less. 
Today, everything is produced en 
masse for the masses, including educa¬ 
tion and recreation. Man is becoming 
homogenized and we are in danger of 
losing those individual freedoms for 
which we fight so staunchly, not to a 
dictator or a government, but to our¬ 
selves, our own mass society. 

When camping began as a recrea¬ 
tional activity, it was carried out in 
small groups under leadership ex¬ 
perienced in the ways of the great out¬ 
doors. It set out to provide oppor¬ 
tunities for boys, and later girls, to 
become self-reliant, to understand the 
ways of nature, and to develop both 
mentally and physically from contact 
with it. Since then, camping has come 
a long way, too far in the opinion of 
many, to the extent that the art of 
outdoor living no longer plays any 
part. Far too often, children going to 
camp are simply transferred from one 
mass to another, where far too much 
is done for them; life is organized 
twenty-four hours a day, and adven¬ 
ture is sterile. Camps are, of course, 
influenced by pressure of the masses. 
Children tend to pass through them 
rather like any other product on an 
assembly belt—they go in white and 
come out uniformly tanned, two 
pounds heavier, and decorated with 
craft strip. I have seen many children 
who would been a lot better off losing 
two pounds at camp, but what would 
Mum have said?; and what a blot on 
camp statistics! This is not a reflec¬ 
tion on camps—(in the main they do a 
good job achieving what is expected 
of them)—so much as a reflection on 
our society that it should encourage 
such results. 

I submit, this is not camping as it 
set out to be—the simple art of living 


outdoors. The art of outdoor living is 
basic and does not change. Only we 
in our conceit have substituted tech¬ 
nique for art and short cuts for work, 
and deceive ourselves the result is the 
same. A recent article in the Peter¬ 
borough Examiner headed. “Outdoor 
Man Mastered Fire-making Without 
Smoke, Sweat or Tears”, listed an in¬ 
credible number of modern articles de¬ 
signed to alleviate the chore of outdoor 
cooking and concluded with the follow¬ 
ing paragraph — “Outdoor eating, 
thanks to the inventors, has now. be¬ 
come almost as scientifically thrilling 
as indoor eating. In fact, you might 
want to rough it some day by going 
back indoors for a summer meal.” 

After we had overcome our amaze¬ 
ment on top of that Ghiltern Hill I 
mentioned earlier, we went down into 
the valley to find a camp site for the 
night. The first farmer we approached 
greeted us with “Have you heard the 
news? It has just been announced on 
the radio that Lord Nuffield has offered 
to donate $50,000 to the Boy Scouts 
Association providing they raise an 
equal amount by their own efforts.” 
This was terrific news and we came 
right back, “O.K., what can we do for 
you?” which apparently was what he 
expected. We spent a wonderful week¬ 
end camping and working on that 
farm, went to church with the farmer 
and his family and shared an enormous 
supper with them before we left with 
our contribution towards the $50,000. 
Stevenson concluded, “To travel hope¬ 
fully is a better thing than to arrive” 
with “and true success is to labour”, 
and that, whole quotation sums up the 
spirit of the art of outdoor living. 

What then is the art of outdoor liv¬ 
ing? It is the ability to live comfort¬ 
ably out of doors by your own efforts— 
to be able to make the most of what 
you have and can find around you— 
to raise your hat to all you meet, to 


Toronto , Canada , December 1958 


15 



be able to commune with nature and 
to appreciate the works of God. (Don’t 
misunderstand me—I am not suggest¬ 
ing a cult of nature worship). 

Practising the art of outdoor living, 
a person gets away from the masses 
and becomes a thinking individual who 
must make decisions and act for him¬ 
self. These lessons build up confidence 
and self-reliance; ingenuity and powers 
of observation are greatly increased, and 
physical, mental and spiritual well¬ 
being is engendered. Its accomplish¬ 
ment provides a serenity with which 
to combat the strain of the rat race of 
modem day living. 

How are we to bring about an 
awareness of the joys of outdoor living 
in our youngsters through our Gamps? 
First, we must change our organiza¬ 
tion and stop thinking in mass opera¬ 
tions for large numbers. We must make 
our organization much more elastic so 
that it can be quickly adapted to cir¬ 
cumstances and the individual. We 
must provide for the youths in our 
camps to live and work together in 
small groups (and by small groups I 
mean not more than six) and to get 
away from the crowd. I do not agree 
that one of the purposes of camping is 
to teach children togetherness. Most of 
them are always together, they are 
rammed down each other’s throats 
every day in the city, in the suburbs, 
and at school. Gamp is the place to 
teach them the harder lesson, to live 
with a few, to do things alone and 
stand on their own feet. They must 
learn by doing, by active participation. 

I would like to give you what I 
think is an excellent example of the 
powers of influence of outdor living. 
As a young Scoutmaster I was asked 
to take in John, a delinquent, whom 
the Juvenile Court felt could be helped 
by Scouting. When I first met this boy 
he frightened me; he was one of those 
real hard customers who the unen¬ 


lightened would say was bad through 
and through. He attended meetings 
but did not seem to benefit from them; 
he was rebellious and always wanted 
to be doing something different from 
the current activity. One weekend, I 
took him with three other boys and 
my dog, on a long weekend boat trip 
up the middle reaches of the Thames. 
As soon as he knew we were going to 
travel by punt he was scornful, and 
wanted to use a power boat so we 
could zip up to Reading and back in 
no time flat. 

“Where are we going? What are we 
going to do?” 

“Oh, just punt upstream and see 
what happens”. 

“Pooh!” 

It was Springtime and we cruised 
up close to the banks watching birds on 
nests, and young voles having their first 
lessons in the water. At the whim of 
one of the boys we turned up a little 
backwater, dodging dead heads, duck¬ 
ing under low branches, until suddenly 
rounding a bend, we came right upon a 
swan sitting on its nest. The swan 
made no bones about its feelings, rose 
straight up hissing and came straight 
for us with its huge wings beating. 
It could have been a nasty situation 
but the dog in the bows rose to the oc¬ 
casion. The boy who was stroke paddle 
gave clear quick orders and the others, 
John included, as quickly carried them 
out as we backed away from danger. 
From that time on John seemed to 
change—for the rest of that trip he was 
more co-operative and appeared to take 
more interest in what was going on. 
As the months passed he seemed to 
soften up and although I left that dist¬ 
rict soon after, the last I heard he had 
became a most successful Leader. It 
is, of course, hard to say exactly what 
it is that does affect boys but I feel 
sure that that trip was a turning point 

continued on page 43

Canadian Camping 



AND AROUND WE GO .. . 

A welcome contribution from 
DON COWAN , General Secretary, 
New Westminister f B.C., Y.M.C.A. 



As an ex-camp director who has 
been shoved off into administrative 
work in the city, I am continually fas¬ 
cinated by the regular change in em¬ 
phasis in our own boys’ and girls’ 
camp. We swing gaily back and forth 
from the tightly scheduled activity pro¬ 
gramme to a wide open permissive 
structure. Each new tack seems to be 
a reaction from the previous, and in 
my twelve years of association with 
this particular group we seem to have 
gone the full circle. I shall be very care¬ 
ful in these comments not to let you 
know at which point I was camp direc¬ 
tor. so you will have to guess which 
particular jag I was on! 

I hope I do not offend the pro¬ 
ponents of any particular type of camp¬ 
ing here, but I might say we have had 
all kinds. We have had the types who 
reacted against the transplanting of 
city programme to a country setting, 
and his reign would be characterized 
by the banning of bats* balls and ath¬ 
letic equipment, and the exaltation of 
the hatchet and knife. Another time 
we had one of these Phys. Ed. boys who 
robbed our gym in the city of all its 
portable sporting equipment for the 
camp programme. A case worker took 
the helm once, and every boy was care¬ 
fully tested, investigated, recorded, re¬ 
ported, documented and segmented, 
and all this material went into a fat 
dossier. We have also had our jags 
of being Cowboys, of being Indians, of 
being Trappers. 

Each time a new trend in program¬ 
ming was launched, its champion did 
so with fanatical zeal, sometimes ac¬ 


companied with a strong condemnation 
of contrary programme philosophies. 
The number of arguments about how 
camps should be handled is possibly 
second only to the number of argu¬ 
ments that develop in a parent’s group 
on how youngesters should be brought 
up at home. 

Maybe we should have saved our 
breath to cool our porridge—for talk¬ 
ing to the campers of various seasons 
and watching their progress into young 
adulthood, there was no indication that 
any specific programme philosophy or 
director topped the other. They loved 
’em all! 

I am reminded of a story which is 
not intended as a reflection on scientific 
camping but as a reminder to us all to 
keep our eye on the camper. It con¬ 
cerns young Johnnie who had been at 
camp for almost a week but refused 
to participate in the active programme 
with his fellow campers. This was a 
great concern and worry to the director 
and his staff and they finally called a 
conference of the top brass to discuss 
the situation. They discussed the re¬ 
port on his I.Q., his P.Q., his medical 
report, his home background. Was he 
rejected by his parents? Had he had 
a traumatic experience in early child¬ 
hood? etc., etc. Finally a junior Coun¬ 
sellor was passing by and overheard 
the conversation so he said, “You want 
to know what’s the matter with John¬ 
nie? Just a minute—I’ll ask him.” The 
C.I.T. trotted over, and after a few 
words of earnest conversation with the 
boy—came back and said: 

“His shoes hurt.” —• 


Toronto, Canada , December 1958 


17 


MARGARET GOV AN, after reading the 
controversial article in MacLean’s Magazine, 
sat down to assess camping values which she 
felt were almost entirely lacking in the 
article . . . and this is the result. 


BECAUSE 


I believe that a term at a good camp, 
can be an invaluable experience for the 
normal boy and the normal girl. 

Because I believe that a boy should 
learn the out-door skills and learn them 
properly . . . for the fun they can give 
him, for the satisfaction of learning 
such skills, and the making use of his 
body, for the self-confidence which re¬ 
sults. These skills, by and large, are 
those of the pioneers, and are the right¬ 
ful heritage of the child of to-day. And 
camps have more facilities, more 
trained personnel, for teaching these 
skills than is usual elsewhere. 

Because I believe that a boy needs to 
come to grips with natural environment 
. . . to realize his relationships with all 
living things, the pattern of life, the 
power of the elements—so that he will 
respect, work with, and relate himself 
to the world of nature. 

Because I believe that a boy should 
learn to wonder and to worship. In 
the more primitive life, close to nature, 
with wise guidance, boys can learn to 
marvel. City boys, especially, can re¬ 
turn to the world as it was created, 
and from wonder move to worship of 
the Creator. 


I BELIEVE . . . 


Because I believe that a boy needs to 
experience a simpler type of living than 
goes on in the large cities . . . without 
the clutter of the community with all 
its rush and bustle, T.V., movies, radio, 
comic books, advertising, noise, shops 
traffic, infinitum . . . and to go apart, 
for a time at least, to live in the out- 
of-doors where life moves at a slower 
pace, with less distractions, less com¬ 
petition, less tension. In such a situa¬ 
tion, again with wise guidance, a lad 
can see more clearly, can find his direc¬ 
tions, can set up standards for himself. 

Because I believe that a boy is being 
gypped of his birthright if he is not 
given the opportunity to develop a 
philosophy of life ... a religion to live 
by. In camp where experiences are 
common to all and the span of age and 
interest is restricted, religion can be 
closely related to living experiences. 

Because I believe that a boy should 
be brought into contact with wide in¬ 
terests, hobbies, crafts, the work of the 
artist, be it painting, music, poetry, 
what-have-you. A camp can make our 
culture and heritage available through 
its campfires and programme. 


18 


Canadian Camping 


Because I believe that a boy should 
be provided with the treasure of good 
memories . . . and camp can provide 
them: starlight paddles, the thrill of 
catching a fish, sunsets and dawns, the 
sight of a moose, stories worth remem¬ 
bering, achievement and participation 
in sports, dew sparking on cobwebs, 
friendships, music, good adventure. 

Because I believe that a boy should 
experience, at some time in his life, 
the fun and laughter, the happiness of 
a holiday planned for him, full of free¬ 
dom to be himself, interest, satisfaction, 
and accomplishment suited to his 
capabilities; and again camp can pro¬ 
vide an atmosphere, a climate where 
these can flourish. 

Because I believe that a boy should 
be given time and opportunity to make 
friends; and camp gives both . . . and 
also a variety of persons from whom to 
choose friends. In the informal, recrea¬ 
tional setting, hearts are worn on sleeves 
and friendships grow like magic bean¬ 
stalks. The sharing of all kinds of life 
situations, the working and playing and 
living together, offer opportunity un¬ 
limited for knowing each other, under¬ 
standing each other, and liking each 
other. 

Because I believe a boy should know 
young adults, other than his parents. 
If he is surrounded by mature, com¬ 
petent counsellors of varied back¬ 
grounds and experiences . . . the kind 
of young men you hope your son will 
grow up like ... he is sure to identify 
himself with some of them. 

Because I believe that every boy re¬ 
quires objective love and understanding 
. . . and so often it is impossible for 
parents to provide such since they them¬ 
selves are too emotionally involved . . . 
a good counsellor can and does supply 
both. 


Because I believe that every indi¬ 
vidual must have an opportunity to 
measure himself, in all aspects of ex¬ 
perience, with other individuals, in 
order that he may discover himself. 

Because I believe that every in¬ 
dividual must be given the opportunity 
to experience ‘community* ... by which 
I mean the loosing of himself within 
the group, the identifying himself with 
the group, the sharing in the life of a 
group by contributing to its well-being 
... if he is to become the kind of citi¬ 
zen we need. 

Because I believe that a boy should 
experience ‘democratic living* . . . toler¬ 
ance, accepting responsibility for the 
good of the whole, sharing in work, 
learning to respect law and order, 
planning together, the give and take, 
the self-discipline for the sake of the 
freedom of others as well as oneself. 
The communal living in camp can 
teach such lessons par excellence. 

Of course, many of these ‘purposes’ 
can be achieved through other means 
than a term spent at a camp, but a good 
camp is in a unique position in that it 
presents opportunity for all such learn¬ 
ing experiences in a situation which 
claims a boy’s allegiance and interest. 
For this reason a camp staff is enabled 
to offer freely, a boy more prepared to 
accept. 

Again, all of this does not happen to 
any one person, but each camper who 
arrives at camp presents a challenge to 
the camp and staff to accomplish some 
of these objectives. 

And so I believe in camp. 

— • 


Toronto, Canada, December 1958

BILINGUALISM 

IN 

CAMP 


-by Ellen and Axel Carstensen, Directors, 

Camp Edgehill House, 

Brome Lake, Foster, Quebec 


We have always wondered why child¬ 
ren in the Provinec of Quebec as a rule 
do not speak both English and French, 
even when leaving High School after 
six or seven years of instruction. Only 
a very few are able to carry on a con¬ 
versation in the second language. Our 
own two children, who are of just aver¬ 
age intelligence, have spoken three lan¬ 
guages since babyhood. They spoke 
Danish to us at home, French to the 
maid, and English to their playmates. 

We came to Canada over thirty years 
ago, and have laways lived in districts 
where we had both English and French 
neighbours, most of them able to speak 
only their own language. We respect 
and admire both groups, and feel that 
if they all could speak both languages, 
many misunderstandings would be 
avoided. Therefore, when we started 
our camp five years ago, it seemed only 


natural that we should use both lan¬ 
guages in our programme. 

We started with sing-songs, but are 
now at the stage where we use English 
and French in most activities. In order 
to do that, most of our staff are bilin¬ 
gual, and we have children of both 
groups in our camp. It would be very 
easy, if we could follow the method of 
adult study groups, where only the 
second language is spoken, but it is 
difficult enough in the first place for a 
child to adjust to camp life. Imagine a 
child, who wants to tell about his excit¬ 
ing experience, his troubles or some¬ 
times homesickness, not being able to 
speak in his own language, but has to 
search for words to express his feelings 
in a strange language. 

Most children feel that when they are 
in camp they are on vacation; they 
want to have a good time and forget 
all about studies. That silly idea of 
learning French or English was not 
theirs but that of their parents! How¬ 
ever, when the two groups are in camp 
in all activities', they just cannot help 
learning from each other, especially 
among the seniors. 

Although you will hear them ask: 
“How do you say this?” or “How do 
you say that?”, the only times when it 
is compulsory for the children to use 
the second language are: 

(a) for sing-songs. We have one 
after every meal, half English and half 
French. After four weeks of camp, the 
English-speaking children know by 
heart over thirty French songs, includ¬ 
ing verses and the meaning; the French- 
speaking children have learned even 
more English songs. 

(b) at mealtime. Meals are served 
cafeteria style, and each child must ask 

con tinned on page 36

FROM MANITOBA . . . 

One of the highlights of a quick 
trip to Winnipeg was an all-too-short 
chat with Mrs. E. J. Sokol, President 
of the Manitoba* Camping Association, 
and Miss Marian Searles who have 
much in the way of good news to re¬ 
port about the Manitoba Association. 
Latest records show an encouraging 
increase in membership, which only 
substantiates a keen spirit of enthu¬ 
siasm in all their projects, and opti¬ 
mism for the future. We expect to 
have further reports of their work for 
this year, as well as one or two articles 
on some types of camping in that pro¬ 
vince. 

Our good wishes go with you Mani¬ 
toba!

Toronto , Canada, December 1958 


21 



The Cad 
of Algonquin 


We are grateful to Mr. Hart Devenney, Director of the Bark Lake 
Ontario Camp Leadership Centre, for submitting this tribute to a new 
book by Miss Hamilton, internationally-known former camp director, 
and beloved member of the Ontario Camping Association. 


This is a most interesting book, writ¬ 
ten by an interesting person about an 
interesting camp. As one proceeds 
from chapter to chapter the impression 
grows that a history of the camping 
movement in the Province of Ontario 
has been given us; a history from the 
pen of an author with a philosophy of 
life which puts the development of 
people before the development of 
elaborate facilities. 

Many, of course, of the procedures 
which Miss Plamilton decided upon in 
the Camp Tanamakoon programme 
have now become staridard as far as 
organized camps are concerned. The 
important point is that she was one of 
the pioneers. 

There is a challenge, too, in the story 
of the early days of her camp. How 
the treks into the Algonquin wilder¬ 
ness brought to a neophyte an apprecia¬ 
tion of .nature which was not present 
before; how the beauty which was 
placed on canvas by the painter Tom 
Thomson came alive; and how the first 
primeval was overcome by the deter¬ 
mined devotion of a self-created prob¬ 
lem; all these things are portrayed for 
us in broad, vivid, even sometimes 
repetitive paragraphs. 

At the end of the chapter “Learning 
to live in a Community”, Miss Hamil¬ 
ton has used a short extract called 
“What is Camp.” This more than 
stimulating piece of writing epitomizes 
what the founder of Tanamakoon was 


working for as she sometimes plodded, 
sometimes tripped gaily along and 
sometimes bounded along the path of 
camp history. Most certainly this pro¬ 
cedure adopted over the years was one 
of effectiveness without stale overtones. 
There was change when necessary but 
not necessarily. Learning by doing was 
practiced throughout the campers’ stay 
with Miss Llamilton but not without a 
realization that there was a community 
of purpose as well as community in 
living. 

When she recounts for the reader 
the policies and procedures which were 
to become guides for the work-a-day 
programme, she is not telling of some 
bloodless blueprint conceived from 
above and handed down. The Tana¬ 
makoon counsellor’s Guide was, and 
likely is still, a “co-operative effort of 
the Counsellors.” “It grew as we grew” 
says Miss Hamilton, and it was “revised 
each year.” The continuity of service 
given to the camp by the counselling 
staff contributed, no doubt, to this. 
The whole process may be described as 
the on-going work of an in-service 
training programme. 

Loyalty of staff to camp standards 
was primary of course, but by making 
the individual responsible for the main- 
tenance of accepted standards, 
campers, counsellors and staff alike, 
a mutual understanding of policies and 
procedures ensued. The inclusion of 
the camper in this process is the im- 


22 


Canadian Camping 









portant point here, h ecause too 
often campers, or pupils, fpr that 
matter, are not put “before principles.” 
No play on words is intended here. It 
is a real educationist who would “try 
to see the possibilities in the child 
(camper or what have you) by looking 
through her faults to the person you 
think she could be. 

By separating her book into four 
parts, Miss Hamilton has made it easy 
for a reviewer to look for the highs 
and the lows in Camp Tanamakoon’s 
history. Thus, if one were to stop at. 
the end of the second . section one 
would have gained only the idea that 
here was idealism run rampa,nt. But 
when she moves into section three and 
discusses programme, the means by 
which the idealism is put to work is 
broadly sketched; for as the first sen¬ 
tence of the section suggests “The fun 
and the achievement of camp, of the 
friendship, adventure and daring (de¬ 
pend) to a large extent on the daily 
programme of activities.” 

From an administrative standpoint 
the relation of specialist counsellors to 
the various sections of programme 
presents problems which many camps 
are now meeting by eliminating the 
“specialist” and having all counsellors 
give leadership to all phases of pro¬ 
gramme. The main problem suggested 
at this point is that the specialist tends 
to concentrate on the speciality and 
sometimes over-emphasizes it or fails 
to see the broader picture of camping 
and the objectives thereof, or has diffi¬ 
culty fitting into the staff family pic¬ 
ture because of the exclusiveness of 
interest in the specialty. 

This also presents the greatest prob¬ 
lem for the smaller organization, 
church, or agency camps, since it in¬ 
volves increased counsellor salary costs. 

A very salient, if not poignant ob¬ 
servation is made by the author in 
regard to nature study which, to this 
reviewer’s thinking, should be part and 


parcel of all camping programmes, that 
it has not always been possible to find 
enough counsellors competent to find 
and explain the wonders that lie 
around us in the woods. The question 
this always raises: do we need the 
specialist here, or do we need coun¬ 
sellors who can see the opportunities 
which even an elementary knowledge 
of nature affords, is paramount for all 
camp directors. 

The story of Camp Tanamakoon is 
the story of one camp. It might also 
be the story of many camps which, over 
the years, have been exceptional in 
their influence. It is significant that 
the camping movement has been des- 
ribed in “The Call of Algonquin” as 
a new venture in education. But it is 
more significant that the author sug¬ 
gests that this new venture “almost by 
accident” was stumbled upon by those 
who have given their lives for the 
movement. 

There are a few 1 things in the com¬ 
position of Miss Hamilton’s book that 
would have helped the camp researcher 
who will want to refer to her work 
frequently. An index at the back 
would be an asset for instance. By 
placing the very excellent pictures 
throughout the book, instead of joining 
them two pages by two pages as now 
arranged, would be a better use of 
them, it is felt. 

But these are only minor points. This 
review can rightfully be closed by again 
saying that “The Call of Algonquin” 
by Mary G. Hamilton is a most inter¬ 
esting book about an interesting camp. 
It is more than the biography of one 
camp alone because the growth and 
development of Camp Tanamakoon is 
also the story of many other camps. 
It is therefore a history of the camping 
movement, and as such can be read 
with pleasure and profit by campers, 
counsellors and parents. 

The Ryerson Press, Toronto. $4. 


Toronto, Canada, December 1958

Canadian Camping 












Mother 

Went 

Comping 


JEAN SHILTON, writing in The United 
Church Observer, looks back at camping 
and gives us a hope for the future. Mrs. 
Shilton, formerly Girls’ Work Secretary for 
the United Church, is the wife of the 
Reverend ]. F. Shilton, of Alliston, Ontario, 
and is the mother of five children. 


I’m just as sticky as the next parent 
when it comes to choosing a summer 
camp for my children. I want to know 
if they will have juice for breakfast, if 
the dishes are rinsed in javex, and if 
the cabins are clean and dry and airy. 
It helps to restore my perspective to 
remember my own camping days before 
javex was invented. 

My first camps were G.G.I.T. Camp¬ 
ing for anyone younger than twelve 
was not frowned upon in our corner of 
Canada. It had never even been 
thought of. It was during the depres¬ 
sion, and I guess a* lot of things about 
those camps were as depressed as our 
economics. The only buildings on the 
campsite were a cookhouse minus all 
conveniences and a couple of other 
small buildings hidden in the bushes. 
We lived in tents, and ate in a large 
tent. On a very hot day the butter 


melted in the saucers on the tables, and 
the dust blew into the dining tent and 
swam in the melted butter. There was 
so much starch in the diet that several 
girls had hives and a few had swollen 
eyelids. 

We washed, and cleaned our teeth in 
the lake. We would laugh scornfully 
at the idea of a wash-house. After all, 
we were Campers, rugged ones. We 
peeled the vegetables for dinner, hauled 
water and split wood. Every evening 
we sat on the hill and sang “Day is 
Dying in the West.” The cynics call it 
sun worship and they may be right. 

But we had leaders at those camps, 
women who were dedicated Christians 
and who liked us girls. Miraculously, 
the Gospels throbbed with new mean¬ 
ing and Christ became a living Leader 
Whom we resolved to follow to the end. 
We sang and we sang, in every spare 
minute of the day, and some of the 
songs I learned there I sing to my 
children now. We became aware of 
beauty and if we worshipped the work 
of the Creator too ardently, we were 
also drawn nearer to the Creator. We 
discovered ourselves at Camp, dis¬ 
covered that our adolescent dreams and 
insecurities and questions were shared 
by others, and discovered that we be¬ 
longed to God. 

The campsite I loved has long since 
been abandoned, but if I could go back 
to it and inspect it on behalf of my 
own children, I should probably be 
shocked by its inadequacy. Never¬ 
theless, the camps there did something 
to my soul from which I have never 
recovered. May the camps with the 
javex and the orange juice and the dry 
cabins do as much for my children. 

—• 


Toronto, Canada, December 1958 


27 




By Dorothy M. Douglas 



SOUNDS FUN! 

Barbara Hill, Anne Smith and 
Dorothy Simpson 

THE SOUNDS FUN CLUB was 
created by the Junior League of Tor¬ 
onto and its adventures and activities 
were presented on radio through the 
co-operation of the CBG as an educa¬ 
tional project for children. From the 
scripts of these programmes the three 
authors have selected the mtaerial for 
this book. The aim of the radio pro¬ 
gramme was to interest children every¬ 
where in all sorts of creative activities 
by helping them to discover how many 
fascinating projects are possible in the 
the everyday world around them. 

The members of the club are between 
nine and eleven years of age. Each 
chapter in the book (which the child¬ 
ren can read or have read to them) 
describes one particular activity of the 
club. The members find themselves a 
meeting place (an old toolshed), a pass¬ 
word, and any number of intriguing 
things to do once they put their 
heads and their energies together. Each 
chapter concludes with specific direc¬ 


tions on how the ideas suggested there 
might be carried out. For the cabin 
counsellor—indeed, for any camp 
counsellor—this book offers excellent 
suggestions for sparking the adventur¬ 
ous spirit of children and giving ex¬ 
pression to their natural creativity. It 
demonstrates how easily a group of 
children can amuse themselves, and 
how they develop socially in a little 
friendship club such as this. 

Clarke, Irwin & Company Ltd., 
Toronto. $3.50. 

NATURE IS YOUR GUIDE 

Harold Gatty 

Without doubt this book will fas¬ 
cinate all outdoorsmen—whether they 
be hunter, fisherman, explorer, sailor, 
climber, or camper. The author’s aim is 
to enable the reader to find his way on 
land or at sea, if necessary, without map 
or compass, by using one’s powers of 
observation and by knowing how to 
interpret the signs of nature. He main¬ 
tains that nature places countless clues 
and guide-posts at our disposal as aid? 
to pathfinding and navigation, and 
that with a little practice we can read 


28 


Canadian Camping 



them as clearly as if they were street 
signs. 

Gatty was born in Tasmania and 
now lives in the Fiji Islands. As a 
member of the merchant marine and 
of the Royal Australian Air Force he 
became a keen navigator and has car¬ 
ried out reserach in navigation for 
more than thirty-five years on journeys 
all over the world. In one chapter he 
recounts how early man found his 
way by observing, among other things, 
the flyways or migratory routes of 
birds, by watching the movement of 
stars, using their eyes and ears to learn 
the phenomena of nature. Lord Baden 
Powell built his Scouting movement on 
watching and listening, on developing 
keen faculties of observation. These 
are necessary in finding direction, tel¬ 
ling time, returning to one’s base or 
home without getting lost. While today 
technical aids such as the compass, the 
sextant, maps, weather stations are 
very efficient, situations can arise when 
it is vital for us to be able to hnd our 
way with only nature as our guide. 

The book contains chapters on these 
natural signposts fashioned by the 
wind, the sun, the moon, the sky, trees 
and plants, even anthills. In special 
chapters he discusses finding one’s 
way in towns, on the desert, in polar 
regions, at sea. The camp hike and 
canoe trip offer wonderful opportuni¬ 
ties to develop a knowledge of natural 
methods of pathfinding and orienta¬ 
tion. A great deal of pleasure can be 
derived from an otherwise uneventful 
walk in the country or cruise on the 
water by studying nature’s signposts. 
How many of us can find our way out 
of a forest, across country, or back to 
shore from open water in an emer¬ 
gency? 

Collins, Don Mills, Ontario. $3.50. 

EIGHTY LAND BIRDS TO KNOW 

If you like to do a bit of bird-watch¬ 
ing, you will know that a compact 


reference book which slips easily in and 
out of a jacket pocket or knapsack is 
a boon companion. This is one. At 
the front of the book is a colour key 
to the male spring plumage of the 
eighty birds. When a bird you are 
stalking gets within range of your 
binoculars or the naked eye, you try 
quickly to note its salient character¬ 
istics before it hops, runs, or flys away. 
With Thompson’s key you can recog¬ 
nize the parts of the bird you were 
able to observe, and if you have con¬ 
firmed enough characteristics to 
identify the bird you then turn up the 
page on which it is more fully de¬ 
scribed. The key shows colour patches 
of each bird’s head, back, wing, tail, 
breast and sides, and in two or three 
words suggests its habitat and general 
impression. All of these land birds may 
be seen in Ontario and adjoining pro¬ 
vinces. Birds seen only in Western 
Canada are not shown. Campers whose 
observations take place among the 
northern lakes might miss the water 
birds here. For them we suggest that 
this splendid ninety-page reference 
book, with its suggestions on how to 
watch birds, be supplemented with the 
National Museum’s set of fifty Can¬ 
adian bird cards (series A) which in¬ 
cludes water birds and is obtainable 
from the Museum or the Queen’s 
Printer at Ottawa for $1. Many mem¬ 
bers of the Canadian Camping Asso¬ 
ciation know Mr. Thompson as an en¬ 
thusiastic and reliable naturalist. The 
Book Society of Canada, Agincourt, 
Ont. $2.25. 

USE YOUR LEISURE 

Guy R. Williams 

A Book or Pastimes for boys and 
girls of ten ^ears and up, it presents 
projects which are described in full 
detail with diagrams to illustrate. Mr. 
Williams has written two other books, 
USE YOUR HANDS! on handicrafts, 
and USE YOUR EYES!' on drawing

ALGONQUIN ADVENTURE— 
Ronald J. Cooke 

Boys and girls love an adventure 
s.tory particularly if the setting is in the 
very part of their own country they 
know well; for this reason alone Algon¬ 
quin Adventure will have wide appeal, 
and will even include adults among its 
readers. Its chief value to old and 
young alike lies in the amount of 
authoritative information on sensible 
outdoor living techniques, and the in¬ 
teresting way in which history, nature- 
lore and woodcraft are presented in 
every chapter of the book. We can 
see it as an excellent source of discus¬ 
sion materials as counsellors read it to 
their campers, and a small reference 
book to which campers can refer at any 
time. Mr. Cooke writes in that easy, 
flowing style that helps children read 
quickly to the end of the story. Al¬ 
gonquin Adventure will find its way to 
many a camp library, and should prove 
a favourite with all readers. 

The Ryerson Press, Toronto . $3.50

was accepted and the farm purchased 
for $15,000.00. 

In 1954 the new Quebec Lodge came 
into operation with ample room for ex¬ 
pansion and with pleasing isolation 
from neighbours. With the surplus the 
old farm buildings were renovated to 
suit the needs of the camp including 
the creation of a chapel in the large 
loft of the stable. In the intervening 
years new buildings have been erected, 
one of which is a large recreation hall. 
To-day Quebec Lodge is a hive of ac¬ 
tivity from late June until early Sep¬ 
tember, one group following another; 
boys, girls and young people—well over 
400 in a season—with carefully chosen 
staffs and adequate facilities for every 
possible activity. For Archbishop Car¬ 
rington this growth was a great achieve¬ 
ment and in all its planning he was 
greatly assisted by Mrs. Carrington 
who has shared his enthusiasm for 
camping from their early days in New 
Zealand. 

Quebec Diocese is a tremendous area. 
It covers 280,000 square miles and ex¬ 
tends from the New England border 
out to the Gulf of St. Lawrence and 
includes the Gaspe Peninsula, the 
Magdalen Islands and the north shore 
of the Gulf to Blanc Seblan across from 
Newfoundland. One camp in the west 
is not sufficient for the Diocese. There 
is another venture, Fort Haldimand, 
near the town of Gaspe; here the swim¬ 
ming is in the salt water of the Gulf. 
Like Quebec Lodge, Fort Haldimand 
has grown and developed over the years 
into a splendid and well-equipped camp 
with adequate accommodation for boys 
and girls up and down the coast and 
from the Magdalen Islands. 

Many of them came as Scout and 
Guide units. The growth of Fort Haldi¬ 
mand is due largely to the initiative of 
the clergy and laity of the area, and a 
number of the former got their first

It is not surprising that these long 
years of camping activity have had the

professional team under the leadership 
of Mr. Don Graham, Director of Edu¬ 
cation for Forest Hill Village. 

Saturday Sessions are being planned 
for Counsellors, Activity Heads, Senior 
Staff and Directors.

Toronto, Canada, December 1958 


33 
































Each year more and more Canadian 
families are turning to the out-of-doors 
during the vacation period for relaxa¬ 
tion, refreshment, and simple living 
together. In provinces from coast to 
coast, family groups plan to pack the 
family car at the beginning of holidays, 
and head for some camp-site near or 
far, to taste the joys (they hope) of 
sleeping under canvas, of cooking over 
fire, of fishing in a trout-filled stream, 
or just plain loafing by a quiet wood- 
rimmed lake. 

Family Camping has become a 
major activity for young and old in 
both Canada and the United States in 
recent years. There are many reasons 
for this, but as society becomes more 
irbanized, more automatic, more 
sedentary there will be a corresponding 


tion which has, as one of its functions, 
the provision of camp and picnic sites 
throughout the province. At the end 
of 1957 there were 64 locations in B.C. 
with family camping units ranging 
from one to as high as 150 at any 
one site. Miracle Beach, one of the 
.larger units in B.C. situated on the 
eastern shore of Vancouver Island, had 
over one million visitations in 1956. 
Equally interesting developments could 
he noted for other provinces, especially 
Ontario and the Atlantic provinces. 

Family Camping in the United 
States has reached even larger propor¬ 
tions than in Canada. In the National 
Forests of the U.S. there are 4,400 
camping and picnic sites specially sel¬ 
ected for the convenience and enjoy¬ 
ment of family groups. 280,000 people 


FAMILY 

A NEW TREND . . . 


increase in the number of people who 
will find physical, mental and spiritual 
refreshment in living for a brief period 
each year close to natural things. Per¬ 
haps through this type of activity many 
families will find again the joys and 
satisfactions which come from sharing 
the experiences which come from a 
holiday living under canvas. 

Many government departments are 
now promoting the use of National 
Forests and Federal and Provincial 
Parks by providing picnic and camp¬ 
ing facilities either free of charge or 
for a nominal fee. The supplying of 
camping and outdoor equipment has 
become a major industry in many 
centres with special stores catering 
solely to this activity. British Columbia 
has established a Ministry of Recrea- 


can be accommodated at one time in 
the National Forests. This is in addi¬ 
tion to the many sites found in the state 
parks throughout the U.S. Mention 
must be made of the trail systems 
found in different parts of America. 
These are trails suitable for hiking or 
horseback riding which run through 
the wilderness sections of the country. 
One example is known as the Pacific 
Crest Trail System which runs from 
Canada to the Mexican border a dist¬ 
ance of about 1500 miles. Here a 
family group could ride or hike for as 
long or as short a distance as they 
wish, with areas set aside at suitable 
distances for over-night camping. 

At the present time most family 
camping is done by car. With crowded 
highways and increasing traffic hazards 


34 


Canadian Camping 






and delays, there is a newer trend 
toward marine camping, where the 
family travels by small boat. Already 
in B.C. steps are being taken to pro¬ 
vide camp-sites along the coast and on 
the borders of the larger lakes. 
Another answer to the traffic problem 
is found in the hiking or riding trip, 
where the car is taken to a certain 
spot and left while the trip is continued 
either on foot or on horseback. For 
those who want to get on the less 
frequented roads and byways, the 
trailer type of camping is possible. This 
permits more extended trips with less 
time taken to set up camp each night. 

Therefore, it can be seen that the 
scope of Family Camping embraces 
four types of activity, namely — 

1. Car Camping — under canvas. 


1. Pre-trip Planning. The entire 
family should be brought together 
to discuss the idea of a family 
camping trip. 

Unless everyone in the family is inter¬ 
ested and enthusiastic, it is unlikely 
that the trip will be successful. It may 
be necessary for the enthusiastic mem¬ 
ber, whether it be Mother, Dad, or 
Junior to promote the idea. This pre¬ 
liminary discussion should serve a use¬ 
ful purpose to parents who find it 
difficult to get the family together on 
a common project. If well handled, it 
can result in a strengthening of family 
ties by sharing discussion and ideas. 

2. All members of the family must 
share in the planning. 


CAMPING 


By Lome and May Brown, 

British Columbia Camping Association. 


2. Trailer Camping. 

3. Trail Camping. 

4. Marine Camping. 

The extent to which each of these is 
done will depend on the availability 
of camping facilities, the accessibility 
of sites to large centres of population, 
the existence of trails, and the educa¬ 
tion of the public on the techniques of 
family camping. 

A few suggestions follow that may 
be helpful to those who, as yet, have 
done little, if any, family camping. The 
points given might be considered the 
steps which could be taken in sequence 
to get any family group on the way to 
becoming veterans in the art and 
science of living satisfactorily in the 
out-of-doors. 


Toronto , Canada , December 1958 


The interests and needs of individual 
members of any family may vary con¬ 
siderably. A project of this kind 
means, in order to be completely suc¬ 
cessful, give-and-take on the part of 
all. Father must not always have his 
way, nor must the whole trip be plan¬ 
ned around the interests of the teen-age 
members. Many interesting evenings 
during the winter season can be spent 
by the family group in discussing the 
various ideas presented by every mem¬ 
ber, from the youngest to the oldest. 
If each one’s interests are considered as 
far as possible, and all agree that it 
may not be practical to have every 
wish granted, then the first major step 
in the success of the venture is 
assured.

continued from page 20 

for everything in the second language. 
New campers have a few days to get 
adjusted to this, and feel at home, 
before this rule is applied. They usually 
start by themselves with a little prompt¬ 
ing from the child next in line or from 
the counsellor, and it does not take 
them long to get used to the routine 
which we make more or less detailed de¬ 
pending upon the age of the child. As 
an example: On most Sundays we have 
turkey and ice-cream on the menu. A 
senior camper will ask for white meat 
or dark meat, or both, two kinds of 
stuffing, maybe a bit of skin or a bone, 
a lot or a little, a tiny bit, just a taste, 
gravy, peas, carrots, mashed potatoes, 
and the kind of ice-cream which hap¬ 
pens to be on the menu. Of course, we 
have amusing incidents like asking for 
the whole turkey instead of some; the 


camper who asked for poison for fish 
(in French, fish is spelled with two s’s) ; 
and then there was the French girl 
counsellor who asked for lover instead 
of liver, and still gets teased about it. 

(c) at the table the conversation is 
French one day and English the next; 
and here we try as much as possible to 
place the children in groups so that the 
two are mixed. 

Both languages are used in dancing, 
plays and games, and all the little mis¬ 
takes only add so much more to the fun. 
When we had a mock court in English, 
one of our senior French boys, who 
happens to be an extremely good actor, 
had to resort to the use of his pocket 
dictionary continually to find the legal 
terms in English, and the whole audi¬ 
ence was roaring with laughter over his 
mistakes!

For horseback riding and arts and 
crafts, the children may have their in¬ 
struction in the second language if they 
want it, or if the parents request it; 
and some do; but on the waterfront, 
due to the danger involved, each 
camper is instructed in his own lan¬ 
guage. Last year, we had a weekly 
session where the children would tell 
about the highlights of the week in the 
second language, and it went very well, 
so this year we tried to go a little fur¬ 
ther and had a French instructor to 
take the children in classes from fifteen 
to thirty minutes for conversation. Only 
the seniors were interested in it, how¬ 
ever; the younger children felt that it 
tasted too much like school. This was 
particularly true of the younger boys 
who each year build their own club¬ 
house, tearing it down the next year to 
build a bigger one. They felt they 
could not waste even fifteen minutes of 
their precious time on silly things like 
learning French or English. So, the 
French instructor, who turned out to be 
very handy with carpenter tools, spent 
a few hours with them, working and 
giving them a lot of good tips on build¬ 
ing ... in French! They even found 
out that he was good on camp craft, 
when he helped them build a lean-to 
and a fireplace of fieldstone. So what? 
... if you had to ask how to place the 
next stone or the next branch in French 
or English! 

Neither the parents nor we, ourselves, 
expect a child to become bilingual in 
eight weeks, but if, when leaving the 
camp, a child can go to a store or a 
restaurant and ask for things, or sing 
over thirty songs in a second language, 
we feel that he has accomplished quite 
a bit, and without realizing it, these 
children have learned to live together; 
they have made friends and found that 
they are very much the same as children 
are all over the world.

briber 

Our story for this month has 
been used successfully as a point of 
departure by Barry Lowes at Camp 
Timberlane. Mr. Lowes says: “At the 
All Star football game in Chicago, 
they have one place in the ceremony 
where all the lights are turned off; then, 
at a given signal, everyone lights a 
match. Soldier’s Field is a mammoth 
stadium, and one would think that 
lighting just one little match would be 
silly in such a huge place; but when 
over one hundred thousand people 
light one match each, it is almost as 
light as day. In our ceremony at camp 
every camper was given a birthday 
candle which was lighted to create a 
beautiful atmosphere long remembered 
by campers and staff alike.” 

★ ★ ★ ★ 

Not long ago I heard a story that I 
shall never forget. I may not have 
all the details correct, but the idea 
struck, and that is the important part 
for tonight. The story concerned a 
Spanish nobleman who lived in a castle. 
The land as far as one’s eye could see 
belonged to him. His family was his 
pride, but, of course, the children grew 
up, and one by one they moved out 
of the castle to lands he had given 
them. 

When the last son moved away, the 
nobleman became very lonely. He de¬ 
cided to build a chapel where all of 
them might come to worship together. 
He did not tell his children about his 
plans, but he built a beautiful chapel 
high on the mountainside. From its 
front door one could see the entire 


38 


Canadian Camping 











valley, the castle and all of his child¬ 
ren’s homes. When it was finished, he 
called his children to his home, and 
then took them up the side of the 
mountain to see his new chapel. When 
he asked them how they liked it, he 
could see that they were deeply moved. 
One by one his sons gripped his hand. 
His daughters gave him a kiss. He was 
very happy. 

“The first service will be this Sabbath 
night,” he announced. “We will gather 
as the sun sets beside the mountain.” 

Then one of his daughters noticed 
that there were no lights in the chapel. 

“Father,” she cried, “you forgot to 
put lights in the chapel. How can we 
meet at night?” 

But the father answered, “No daugh¬ 
ter, I did not forget the lights. Each 
of you shall be a light.” As he was 


speaking, he walked to a closet, and 
came out with hand lanterns for each 
son and daughter. He passed them 
out to the family, saying: 

“Each of you shall carry this light 
as you come to the chapel. It will 
light your way here, and your return. 
There are holders in the chapel where 
each of you will put the light during 
the service. Remember, if anyone of 
you is missing, the chapel will have just 
that much less light, because of your 
absence. We need the lights of all for 
the perfect chapel light.” 

★ ★ ★ ★ 

That, campers, is just the way we need 
each of you. We would be just that 
much weaker if any of you were ab¬ 
sent. We are certainly glad all of you 
are here.

continued from page 35 

3. Each member of the family should 
be assigned specific and definite 
responsibilities both in preparing 
for the trip and the trip itself. 

These responsibilities must not only 
be assigned, they must be accepted 
willingly and enthusiastically; other¬ 
wise, some aspect of the trip will fail 
with accompanying discomfort and 
possibly dislike for the whole idea. 

4. Assemble literature and informa¬ 
tion on places to go and the type 
of camping facilities that are avail¬ 
able. 

Each one can take on the job of 
writing for, or calling at, places where 
maps and literature are available. This 
can often be done by the school mem¬ 
bers of the family who are anxious to 
put into practice things learned at 
school, such as letter writing. 

5. Plan an easy trial trip over a week¬ 
end prior to the longer vacation 
period. 

No matter how much the idea 
appeals in theory, it is best to actually 
have a trial run at a camp-site within 
easy distance of home. This will show 
up all the problems and the minor 
emergencies which are not serious on a 
short trial run, but could become a 
major factor if they are not found 
until the vacation trip is under way. 
It will let the family know if they are 
really going to enjoy an extended holi¬ 
day of this kind. Most vacation periods 
are too precious to gamble on, thus the 
trial run trip will enable the family to 
evaluate the whole idea. This short trip 
can also be carried out under favor¬ 
able weather conditions, because it will 
be possible to reach the proposed site 


in one day. If the weather is unfavor¬ 
able it is better to stay at home and 
wait for suitable weather. Never take 
a camping trip for the first time in 
poor weather. This will, even with the 
most experienced families, likely bring 
unfavorable reactions to some if not all 
members of the group. 

6. Borrow or rent equipment for the 
first trip. 

It is a mistake, to purchase expensive 
equipment before the family is satisfied 
that this type of activity can bring 
satisfaction and enjoyment to all. 
Improvise as much as possible on such 
things as sleeping bags, and outdoor 
clothing. Rent or borrow a tent and 
learn how to set it up before leaving 
on the trial trip. It is not necessary to 
have a lot of fancy equipment for any 
trip, especially the first ones. Be as 
ingenious as possible. Get a woodlore 
and campcraft book from the local 
library and learn something about the 
woods. Make up useful gadgets and 
see how much fun it can be to get 
along with a minimum of purchased 
equipment. 

7. Food and Cooking. 

Plan simple menus ahead of time. 
Be sure the meals are balanced nutri¬ 
tionally, but do not be too concerned 
about this if the trip is a short one. 
Take a minimum of cooking utensils. 
An ice-box or cooler is perhaps the 
most essential and most important 
piece of camping equipment one can 
have. This could easily be the first 
purchase of any family planning to 
do camping. Ice can be procured in 
most cities and towns of any consequ¬ 
ence. A damp cloth over the cooler will 
preserve the ice and keep the heat out. 
Be sure to buy or make a fairly large 
cooler. It is a mistake to economize and 


40 


Canadian Camping 


think a small one will do. Remember, 
it must hold ice as well as most of the 
food. It is possible to obtain other 
cooling devices for the ice-box, but 
these are not too often satisfactory. It 
is not necessary for Mother to always 
do the cooking. This is an activity all 
can find enjoyable and satisfying. 

Most families use the gas or oil 
stoves for cooking on camping trips, 
and do not depend on wood and the 
open fire for the source of heat. There 
are many places and times when wood 
will not be available, nor will it be 
permissible to light campfires because 
of dry weather or other fire hazards. 
However, it is fun to cook over the 
campfire, and this should be done 
whenever possible. 

8. Plan for the recreation and activity 
of all members of the family when 
on a trip. 

Although everyone will be busy at 
times in the essentials of preparing 
shelter, food, and packing, there are 
periods when each will want to pursue 
activities of his or her own choice. 
Young children should take games and 
reading that will amuse them in event 
of rain. Try to include some reading 
other than comic books. The teen¬ 
agers may want to take the battery 
radio or some other equipment that 
they choose themselves. 

When the weather is fine, there 
is likely to be little trouble in 
everyone being busy, but in the 
event of chilly or wet weather, a 
little foresight will help to pass 
the hours usefully and enjoy ably. 
Books on nature lore and campcraft 
can be tucked in and used to develop 
an appreciation of natural life. Collec¬ 
tions of leaves, stones, insects will often 


be of interest. Studying foot prints and 
the habits of birds and animals will 
often bring real satisfaction to young 
and old alike. Try to make the trip 
one where there is constructive use of 
leisure time. 

9. Safety and Survival in the Out-of- 
Doors. 

The basic fundamentals of first aid 
should be understood by all members 
of the family. The use of such tools as 
axes and knives should be learned by 
all. A compass should be available 
and studied by the family. Basic fun¬ 
damentals of survival should be dis¬ 
cussed and practised. Good safety pro¬ 
cedures should be practised at all 
times. All of these things can be 
carried on both at home before the 
trip and at odd times during the day 
when the trip is underway. 

10. Sanitation and Conservation. 

Most camp-sites have areas set aside 
for the disposal of waste and garbage. 
These should be used with good com¬ 
mon sense and with the full realization 
that someone else will be following you 
at this site. 

The conservation of the natural 
resources of the great out-of-doors is 
one of the major problems facing 
society to-day. As family camping 
increases so will the need for greater 
care in the prevention of fire, in the 
conservation of the trees, the animal 
and birdlife, and the flora and fauna. 
Perhaps one of the most important les¬ 
sons learned from family camping 
will be a greater appreciation of the 
beauties of nature and an increased 
desire to see that these beauties are 
preserved indefinitely. 

continued next page 


Toronto , Canada , December 1958 


41 


continued from page 41 

There are many more things that 
could be said about Family Camping. 
Perhaps these few general remarks and 
suggestions will stimulate a few more 
families to try this living together in 
the out-of-doors. There are many joys 
and satisfactions to be derived from 
living close to nature, because it is 
from this heritage that man came in 
the far distant past. There is still a 
need for all to move away from the 
artificial life of modern society into the 
realm of nature. Perhaps that is the 
reason why Family Camping has 
become part of the culture of life in 
Canada- to-day. It may also be a means 
of restoring some of the essentials of 
desirable family living which are so 
hard to maintain in the society of to¬ 
day.

From Nova Scotia we hear . . . 

From one end of Canada to the 
other, literally, camping Executives, 
YM and YW staff, church workers and 
hosts of other friends can call Mary 
Barker by name, and will be glad to 
hear that she is now living in Ingon- 
ish, Nova Scotia. Always when she 
writes from her house Gaelic-ly named 
Tigh-Na-Mara (Meaning (House-by- 
the-Sea), she includes, characteristi¬ 
cally, snatches of information which 
may have been gleaned from any 
corner of the earth’s surface. Last 
month she included a paragraph: “I 
learned this Grace from a Newfound¬ 
land friend this summer, and thought 
the Editorial Committee might like to 
suggest it as a variation at camps; it 
seems so appropriate in these times: 

“I fold my hands, and bow my head, 
and pray, 

May all the children in the world be 
fed today.”

for John. I also feel quite sure that 
had it been a highly organized trip 
going from A to B with a time 
schedule, and perhaps with three or 
four other boats in the party, we could 
not possibly have had the same fun nor 
found the opportunity which was to 
so influence John. 

Through camping, we have not only 
to bring our youth to an awareness of 
nature, but we must show them how to 
understand it, to enjoy it and to get 
the most from it. To make this possible 
they must be taught from an early age 
how to walk. Walking is fast becoming 
a lost art on the North American con¬ 
tinent and yet it is a simple basic re¬ 
quirement to good health and to enjoy¬ 
ing the art of outdoor living. There is 
a great deal more to walking than just 
putting one foot in front of the other 
and we must show our youth how to 
take care of their feet, what to wear 
and how to walk in broken country. If 
we are going to send them off walking 
or canoeing, we must also teach them 
how to find their way. Again there is 
more to this than the mere technical 
knowledge involved in using a map and 
compass—it means building up a con¬ 
stant awareness of direction and ability 
to read signs. 

They must learn, too, to make them¬ 
selves comfortable in any situation out 
of doors, how to find shelter from the 
elements and how to keep warm day 
and night. Then last, but by no means 
least, they must learn what to eat and 
how to cook it. Of course, there are 
the standard foods to which we are 
used, but if we are to be self-reliant in 
the great out of doors, we must learn 
what foods nature provides locally as 
well. Have you ever sampled boiled 
bracken tip served with melted butter 
on toast? or boiled buttered poke weed, 
or a chunk of salt pork served with
