RARE VISITORS FROM THE SKIES 


A recent news release, on the On¬ 
tario Government, through the Depart¬ 
ment of Lands and Forests, stated that 
a black brant had been taken on the 
Ottawa River. It was shot, during the 
past open season, by a hunter who 
noted that is was unusual and took it 
to the local overseer. It quickly was 
sent to the experts and proved to be 
very rare in the Province. Black brant 
are small geese, about the size of a 
mallard, and are usually sea birds, mi¬ 
grating along the sea coast. Why this 
one wandered into fresh water is not 
known, but sea birds on their migra¬ 
tions will sometimes follow the rivers 
to a point far away from the sea. 

King Eiders and Brunnich’s Murres 
are found every winter on Lake On¬ 
tario. Both species are normally sea 
birds, but follow the St. Lawrence to 
the lake. It is not known for certain 
whether or .not such birds survive and 
return to the sea. There is some evi¬ 
dence that the eiders go back but the 
murres probably perish. Eiders, of 
course, are ducks, but the murres are 
allied to the auks and puffins. 

Western birds make another class of 
rarities in the Province. The whooping 
crane has been in the news for the past 
few years, for there are only 8 or 10 
specimens alive, as far as is known. 
These migrate each year from Texas 
to north of Alberta in the Mackenzie 


district. There is one Ontario-taken 
mounted specimen in Queen’s Museum. 
It was collected at Yarker, near King¬ 
ston, sometime in the eighties, and is 
now at the University for all to see. 

SmaH land birds from the western 
or the southern part of the continent 
have been found in Ontario. The scis¬ 
sor tailed flycatcher has been taken 
once or twice in Northern Ontario 
although its normal home is Texas and 
Mexico. Such waifs probably follow 
the Mississippi valley and go on from 
Lake Winnipeg to Hudson Bay. They 
dislike large bodies of water and Stat¬ 
on the shore line until they reach 
James Bay. The route is only prob¬ 
lematical and the birds may reach 
Moosonee by an entirely different 
route. Very little is known of the move¬ 
ments of stray birds. 

Storms and weather disturbances are 
another hazard for birds of both land 
and sea. Leach’s petrel, a small bird 
that normally is found far out at sea, 
has been taken at Cornwall after a 
severe storm. This, as far as I know, 
is the only Ontario specimen and it is 
now in the Royal Ontario Museum. 
Hurricane Hazel, several year ago, 
brought many birds that are normally 
far to the south at that time. 

Southern birds that reach their ex¬ 
treme northern limits along Lake Erie 
and in New York State, are very often

found in Ontario. There is some evi¬ 
dence that the climate is moderating 
and certainly many a few southern 
birds that were very scare thirty years 
ago, are now found over most of south¬ 
ern Ontario. The cardinal and the 
blue gray gnatcatcher are good 
examples, and the Carolina wren and 
the turkey vulture are others. It may 
interest my readers to know that the 
vulture was recognized at Bancroft in 
1956. 

Some of the heronlike birds have a 
post breeding dispersal that often brings 
them far north of their normal range. 
The American Egret is the best 
example. In late summer, young birds 
are often found in our marshes. Any 
large white wader, nearly as large as 
our heron, will, in all probably, be 
an egret since these birds have in¬ 
creased greatly in the southern States 
with the banning of plume taking.

boiled dandelion leaves and hard boiled 
eggs? or perhaps the greatest of all 
delicacies, barbecued squirrell gar¬

think of the adventure that lies wait¬ 
ing for the cook or gourmet in the 
great out of doors. 

We have a wonderful heritage in our 
land, in this Canada of ours. We, who 
have the responsibility if bringing the 
out of doors within the grasp of every 
child must be sure that we show the 
generations to come how to conserve 
and add to that heritage for all to 
enjoy. No matter where or how they 
travel, they must be sure to meet the 
people, not just superficially, but as 
explorers and fellow artists, so that the 
knowledge and experiences of each may 
enrich the lives of the others. 

The lessons learned in the outdoors 
can mould the pattern for living full 
and purposeful lives and can bring en¬ 
richment to each individual and the

NEW BOOKS FOR YOUNG READERS 


Tenderfoot Trapper. by Arthur Cat her all 

An exciting story of a boy and an old-timer and their adventures in the
